# Takkāriyajātaka (Ja 481)

**ID:** Ja 481
**Section:** Jātaka (ja)
**Collection:** Suttas-Late-1
**Title (Pali):** Takkāriyajātaka
**Title (English, SuttaCentral):** The Student Takkāriya

## AI-generated Overview (from reference literature and SuttaCentral)

*This overview was drafted by an AI model from the cited scholarship and SuttaCentral data and may contain errors; verify against the sources before relying on it.*

The *Takkāriyajātaka* (Ja 481) is a narrative text preserved in the Pali Jātaka collection [SuttaCentral]. According to the traditional introductory frame (*paccuppannavatthu*), the Buddha recounted the story while dwelling at Jetavana in connection with the misguided monk Kokālika, whose slanderous speech against the chief disciples brought about his own ruin [SuttaCentral; Fausböll 1887; Nyanaponika et al. 2003]. In the story of the past, the Bodhisatta was born as the wise young brahmin student (*māṇava*) Takkāriya, a pupil of the royal chaplain (*purohita*) to King Brahmadatta of Benares [Fausböll 1887; Fausböll 1897; Mus 1935]. When the chaplain planned to perform a sacrificial human foundation ritual at the city gate, his own ill-spoken words resulted in his being designated for the sacrifice [Fausböll 1887; Mus 1935]. Takkāriya instructed him with tales demonstrating that unrestrained speech brings destruction, and subsequently spared his master's life by secretly substituting a dead goat for the sacrificial pit [Fausböll 1887; Mus 1935; Sujato 2011]. At the conclusion of the tale, the Buddha identifies the chaplain with Kokālika and himself with Takkāriyapaṇḍita [Fausböll 1887].

In early Buddhist archaeology and art historical studies, a damaged relief at Bharhut depicting a *kinnara* has been identified by B. M. Barua as the *Takkāriya Jātaka*, though other scholars propose the *Candakinnara Jātaka* as an alternative identification [DeCaroli 2004]. The narrative has also received attention in studies of Indian foundation rites and sacrificial reform; Paul Mus examined how the Buddhist redactor adapted an archaic tale of human gate-consecration into an ethical critique of sacrificial cruelty [Mus 1935], a perspective echoed by Bhikkhu Sujato in his analysis of the Bodhisatta's subversion of violent brahmanical sacrifice [Sujato 2011].

According to SuttaCentral, the text exists in four modern translations across four languages [SuttaCentral]. DharmaNexus identifies 19 matching Pali-internal text reuse segments between this text and the *Jātaka-aṭṭhakathā* (Catuttho bhāgo) [DharmaNexus]. For cross-language reuse, DharmaNexus automatically aligns passages of the text with 11 verses in the Buddhist Sanskrit *Patna Dharmapada*, reflecting widespread gnomic verses on the dangers of improper speech [DharmaNexus].
